prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby changing how the gains from trade and the effects of trade policy are understood and measured

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework replaced the representative-firm trade model with productivity-sorted exporters. It created new channels for gains from trade (selection and reallocation) and tied theory directly to firm-level data. The model is a good example of theory that is built to be tested and has been tested repeatedly for more than twenty years across many countries and datasets. It is textbook material and has spread into macroeconomics, IO and development, so maturity is not a concern. The attribution is also workable. Melitz (2003) is the pivotal model, and Helpman, through Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exports versus FDI and his wider trade-theory programme, is the natural second name. After reading the openings I keep this as my first choice, but B009 is a very strong competitor on merit, not only on support.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard and Jensen on exporter premia and Eaton and Kortum on quantitative Ricardian trade have serious priority claims to adjacent parts of the firm-level revolution, and neither is among the credited names. Krugman's 2008 prize already covered the monopolistic-competition foundations, so part of the novelty could be judged to have been rewarded. Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare have also shown that the welfare gains from selection depend on functional-form assumptions and may be smaller than first claimed. A prize here must therefore be framed around selection and reallocation, not around a general claim about gains from trade.

responses.point: B009 is among the most compelling cases on the list. Katz anchors the supply-demand-and-technology framework, Autor the task approach and Hanson the trade-shock evidence, and the evidence is mature and has been tested through replication and debate.
responses.response: I agree that the empirical and conceptual reach of B009 is very strong, and I have it second. I would qualify two points. First, the task framework has other originators, and Goldin (2023) and Acemoglu (2024) were recognised for adjacent work, so the citation would have to be drawn carefully to avoid looking like a topical overlap. Second, B009 combines two strands, skill-biased and task-based technology change and the trade shock, with partly different people behind each. The three-name cap then forces a choice that the evidence does not make obvious. B014 is a single, tighter discovery with a cleaner pair of names. That is why I still put it first, though I would not call the difference large.

responses.point: The B009 proposal is built around the China shock and credits Autor, Hanson and Dorn. Katz is left out because of the three-name limit, and the task framework is treated as secondary.
responses.response: This version is the most defensible way to attribute the trade-shock design, because Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the authors of that evidence. But it moves the prize from a broad account of technology and trade toward one empirical programme, and it drops the long-run skill-premium work for which Katz is the anchor. The other openings that name Katz do the opposite. The disagreement between the two trios shows that B009's credit boundary is less settled than B014's, where nearly every opening names the same pair. I read that as evidence about attribution, not about scientific merit.

responses.point: The B014 case is strong and the framework is ripe, but priority relative to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and to Hopenhayn in firm dynamics, complicates attribution. Whether the quantitative-trade line is the better frame is an open question.
responses.response: I share this concern and it is my main reservation. My answer is that Melitz's contribution is a specific one: a tractable general-equilibrium model in which selection into exporting is endogenous, so that reallocation produces welfare effects. Bernard-Jensen's empirical facts motivated that model, and Eaton-Kortum's Ricardian framework is a different route to quantification. A citation that names selection and firm heterogeneity respects that boundary. I would not extend the prize to the quantitative-trade line, but I accept that this is a judgement the Committee should make explicitly.

responses.point: Melitz and Helpman are the cleanest pair. Redding is more of a later consolidator, and Helpman's separate candidacy (B049) could dilute or complicate his credit.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on leaving Redding out. His quantitative and spatial extensions are important but follow the core discovery. On B049, I would treat it as a question about how the Committee frames Helpman, not as a reason to weaken B014. His contribution to the heterogeneous-firm framework, through the work with Melitz and Yeaple, stands independently of his political-economy-of-trade work, and I would not want to see a single prize carry both.

uncertainties: Whether Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum have claims that the three-name limit cannot accommodate, and whether the Committee would want a configuration that includes them.
How much of the welfare-gain claim survives the Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare critique, which affects how the citation should be worded.
Whether Krugman's 2008 prize for new trade theory makes another trade prize look redundant, and how the Committee should weigh field balance against merit.
Whether B009 should be preferred because its evidence base is broader and the Committee judges the Goldin and Acemoglu overlap to be manageable.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records no co-authorship or institutional tie to any credited name on B014, B009 or B040. Documented connections are limited to long committee overlap with several colleagues and my adjunct appointment at Chicago Booth, neither of which links to these candidates. I rely on the profile and do not claim any independent verification.
